clue.text: Tennyson going to order another drink ? Getting late

definitions.text: Tennyson going to order another drink ? Getting late

parts.words: Tennyson going to order another drink ? Getting late
parts.note: a drinker walks across the pub to the counter for another

explanation.surface: A thirsty poet heads off for one more round as closing time approaches.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's poem 'Crossing the Bar' (1889) is about death, hence 'Getting late'; the pub reading is someone walking over to the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Tennyson's poem about dying also describes walking to a pub counter to buy a drink.

clue.text: Pot plant

explanation.surface: A plant in a pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Pot is slang for the drug hemp, and hemp is also the plant it comes from.

clue.text: Urbanity, that does not cut the 'cackle in Kent

definitions.text: Urbanity, that does not cut the 'cackle in Kent

parts.words: Urbanity, that does not cut the 'cackle in Kent
parts.note: a town in Kent that is also a breed of hen, so a place that keeps up the cackling instead of cutting it short

explanation.surface: Polished manners in Kent that never stop the idle chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: Orpington is a town in Kent (a county in south-east England) and a breed of chicken; 'cut the cackle' is a British idiom for stopping idle talk, but a hen goes on cackling.
explanation.definitionFit: The breed of laying hen is named after the Kentish town where it was developed.

clue.text: Slow it, friend of Stickly Prickly

definitions.text: Slow it, friend of Stickly Prickly

parts.words: Slow it, friend of Stickly Prickly
parts.note: in Kipling's Just So Stories the hedgehog Stickly-Prickly has a tortoise friend whose name is Slow followed by a second word; that word fills the gap

explanation.surface: An instruction to ease off, addressed to a hedgehog's companion.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's 'The Beginning of the Armadilloes' the tortoise is Slow-Solid and the hedgehog Stickly-Prickly; 'it' stands for the missing second half of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The tortoise in Kipling's tale is called Slow-Solid, so the word after 'Slow' completes the hedgehog's friend's name.

clue.text: Mugs one may put one's teeth into ?

definitions.text: one may put one's teeth into ?

explanation.surface: Cups that someone might bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Mugs are fools, which is an old sense of noodles, and noodles are also pasta strands one bites into.

clue.text: See 1
Squabbling sparrows by the way? Not pronouncedly

definitions.text: Squabbling sparrows by the way? Not pronouncedly

parts.words: Squabbling sparrows by the way? Not pronouncedly
parts.note: squabbles among small birds in the bushes would be quarrels of the hedge, but the word for quarrels is not said that way; the real sense is lines of bushes beside a road

explanation.surface: Sparrows bickering at the roadside, though the speaker hints at a trick of saying.
explanation.walkthrough: Rows meaning quarrels rhymes with 'cows'; the bushes lining a lane rhyme with 'rose', hence 'Not pronouncedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines of shrubs bordering a lane or field are what birds such as sparrows nest in by the way.

clue.text: Dip in a scholarly article

parts.note: BA, a Bachelor of Arts, is the degree of a scholarly graduate
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A quick look into an academic paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To dip is to have a short swim or wash in water.

clue.text: Neglectful concerning a single 'one

parts.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
an unmarried woman is addressed as Miss

explanation.surface: Careless about an unmarried person.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone remiss is careless in duty.

clue.text: Demanding in the name of the Crown

definitions.text: in the name of the Crown

explanation.surface: Making a claim on royal authority.
explanation.definitionFit: Demanding means requesting firmly; split as two words it reads 'as king', acting in the monarch's name.

clue.text: Coins ; three of them

explanation.surface: Some money, and a count of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The French gold twenty-franc coins bore the emperor's head, and three French rulers bore the same name.

clue.text: Something given to help mend a tumbledown shack

indicators.note: a shack houses something, so these words hold the letters inside them

explanation.surface: A donation towards repairing a ruined hut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shack' acts as a container: the run lies across 'menD A TUMbledown'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin the word means a thing given, and in English a fact taken as a starting point.

clue.text: Shaded by a beard ?

parts.note: the beard is the bristly tuft on an ear of barley or other grass, so a plant shaded by one has those bristles

explanation.surface: A face half hidden behind whiskers.
explanation.definitionFit: An awn is the bristle at the tip of a grass head, and grain having those bristles is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Those who hang about by the Loire rest curled up

indicators.note: curling up twists something out of shape, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Idlers lounging beside a French river, settling down for a nap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curled up' rearranges LOIRE and REST together; 'by the' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: People who hang about are idlers lingering without purpose.

clue.text: Ruthful and rueful state

parts.note: a condition of being full of pity and sorrow, shown by weeping

explanation.surface: A description of someone full of pity and regret.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone full of sorrow or pity is weeping.

clue.text: Wit that tops all in the House?

definitions.text: Wit that tops all in the House?

parts.words: Wit that tops all in the House?
parts.note: refined wit from ancient Athens, while the room at the top of a house is its first word

explanation.surface: The sharpest humour heard in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the House' looks like Parliament, but it is any house, whose topmost room is the attic.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic salt is a phrase for elegant, pointed wit, named after Athenian style.

clue.text: Government issue of essential oil for a painter

parts.note: GI stands for government issue, also used of US soldiers
otto, also attar, is the fragrant essential oil of roses

explanation.surface: State supply of an aromatic oil to an artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Giotto di Bondone was an early Italian Renaissance painter.

clue.text: Sporting, but not for wear with a deerstalker

definitions.text: Sporting, but not for wear with a deerstalker

parts.words: Sporting, but not for wear with a deerstalker
parts.note: an outfit worn for athletics, although its name suggests a costume for following deer tracks to go with a hunting cap

explanation.surface: Sportswear that would look wrong with a Sherlock Holmes hat.
explanation.walkthrough: A deerstalker is the peaked tweed cap linked to Sherlock Holmes and to stalking deer; tracking deer suggests a 'track suit'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracksuit is a loose outfit worn by athletes when training.

clue.text: Sent the fine, perhaps — unless it was this ?

definitions.text: Sent the fine, perhaps — unless it was this ?

parts.words: Sent the fine, perhaps — unless it was this ?
parts.note: one sense is posted payment of a penalty; the other is a penalty cancelled, in which case nothing would be paid

explanation.surface: Someone paid a penalty, unless it had been let off.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit is both to send money and to cancel a debt or penalty.

clue.text: Such the problem of speed of our wooden walls?

definitions.text: Such the problem of speed of our wooden walls?

parts.words: Such the problem of speed of our wooden walls?
parts.note: the wooden walls are old sailing warships, whose speed is reckoned in nautical miles per hour

explanation.surface: A puzzle about how fast the old navy could go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wooden walls' is a old name for the Royal Navy's wooden warships; their speed is measured in knots, and a hard problem is described with the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A knotty problem is a tangled, difficult one.

clue.text: Their stuff can't last, said the Bard

definitions.text: Their stuff can't last, said the Bard

parts.words: Their stuff can't last, said the Bard
parts.note: Shakespeare's song in Twelfth Night says young people's quality is a stuff that will not endure

explanation.surface: Shakespeare declaring that some material is not built to last.
explanation.walkthrough: Feste's song in Twelfth Night ends 'Youth's a stuff will not endure'; the clue makes the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Young men are the subject of Shakespeare's line that youth will not endure.

clue.text: Relieve as could be ourselves' turning to senility

indicators.note: turning round makes the word for ourselves read backwards

parts.note: us means ourselves
age stands for old age and decline

explanation.surface: Easing a worry about our own drift into dotage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses US to give SU between AS and AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve pain or worry is to soothe and lessen it.

clue.text: All right in oneself and in the mood of…

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in tells us the letter for right goes inside the word for oneself

parts.note: the ego is the self

explanation.surface: Feeling fine in oneself, in a cheerful state of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 22: Milton's poem L'Allegro is about the cheerful mood and contains 'The frolic wind that breathes the spring'.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the marking means brisk and lively, and Milton's poem of that title celebrates the cheerful temperament.

clue.text: : Milton's ." wind that breathes the spring .

definitions.text: : Milton's ." wind that breathes the spring .

parts.words: : Milton's ." wind that breathes the spring .
parts.note: a line from Milton's L'Allegro with one word missing, the adjective for playful that describes the spring wind

explanation.surface: A line of Milton about a spring breeze, with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in Milton's line 'The frolic wind that breathes the spring', carrying on from 21 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The word here means merry and playful, used as an adjective of the wind.

clue.text: Replenish store of what goes on board on board

definitions.text: Replenish store of what goes on board on board

parts.words: Replenish store of what goes on board on board
parts.note: restocking food, the things put on the table or board, while aboard a ship

explanation.surface: Restocking a ship's food supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'board' is a table holding food and also a ship's deck; victuals are provisions.
explanation.definitionFit: To revictual is to supply again with food, the provisions laid on the board.

clue.text: Collaborative H20

explanation.surface: A shared chemical formula.
explanation.definitionFit: Vichy France collaborated with Nazi Germany, and Vichy is also a well-known bottled mineral water.

clue.text: Eastern cutter backed, to trouble this kingdom

indicators.note: backed means sent backwards, so both pieces together are read in reverse

parts.note: to irk is to trouble or annoy
UK is the United Kingdom, the setter's own country

explanation.surface: An Oriental blade supported, in order to cause Britain some bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns IRK + UK as one run into the curved Gurkha knife.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gurkhas of Nepal carry a curved knife, a cutting weapon from the East.

clue.text: Blows of arms and feet

parts.note: the arms are firearms, whose recoil jolts the shoulder, and the feet strike out at things

explanation.surface: Punches and blows from limbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arms' looks like limbs, but it means guns, whose recoil is called the kick.
explanation.definitionFit: A kick is the recoil of a gun and a blow with the foot.

clue.text: Poetic Gray in Italy ?

parts.note: Wordsworth's poem Lucy Gray names a girl whose first name in Italian has this form

explanation.surface: The poet Thomas Gray on an Italian tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gray' suggests the poet Thomas Gray, but it is Wordsworth's 'Lucy Gray'; Italians write Lucy as Lucia.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucia is the Italian form of the girl's name Lucy.

clue.text: Where Justice chiefly should be looked up to

definitions.text: Where Justice chiefly should be looked up to

parts.words: Where Justice chiefly should be looked up to
parts.note: the senior civil court of England, presided over by judges with the title Justice, and literally a raised court

explanation.surface: The place where justice ought to be held in highest esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lord Chief Justice heads the senior courts of England; 'looked up to' points to something elevated.
explanation.definitionFit: The High Court of Justice is the superior court where senior judges sit.

clue.text: You get no footing in the fold, wolf

indicators.note: in places the shortened word inside the enclosure

parts.note: a cote is a shelter or fold for sheep or doves

indicators.note: the foot of a word is its last letter, so it is dropped

parts.note: taken as written before losing its foot

explanation.surface: A wolf warned it will find no foothold among the sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get no footing' cuts the last letter from YOU, leaving YO, which goes in COTE.
explanation.definitionFit: The coyote is the prairie wolf of North America.

clue.text: Stays around'

parts.note: stays are stiffened undergarments, so wearing them around the body means being fitted with one

explanation.surface: Lingers nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: Stays are a corset, so to be in stays is to wear a corset.
